title: Check: Secrets
description: Five questions on Secrets and what they do and do not protect.

questions.prompt: How is Secret data stored in the object itself?

options.text: base64-encoded, which is encoding and not encryption

questions.explanation: base64 is trivially reversible. Anyone who can read the Secret can read its contents - which is why RBAC matters more than the encoding.

questions.prompt: What actually protects Secrets at rest in etcd?

options.text: An EncryptionConfiguration on the API server

questions.explanation: `--encryption-provider-config` on kube-apiserver encrypts resources before they reach etcd. Without it, etcd holds them in the clear.

questions.prompt: Write the command that creates a Secret named db-cred with username=admin.
questions.explanation: `generic`, `docker-registry` and `tls` are the three subcommands worth knowing.

questions.prompt: You run `kubectl get secret db-cred -o yaml`. What do you see under data?
questions.explanation: `kubectl get secret x -o jsonpath='{.data.username}' | base64 -d` is the round trip worth memorising.

questions.prompt: Which of these reduce Secret exposure? Choose all that apply.

options.text: RBAC that restricts who can get secrets
Mounting as a volume rather than an env var

questions.explanation: Env vars leak into `kubectl describe`, crash dumps and child processes; a mounted file is the tighter option. The name protects nothing.
